extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, logic, and metaphysics (readers of induction/causation theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Clarify and apply a philosophical account of causation and laws of nature: identifying what counts as a cause, distinguishing conditional vs. unconditional sequence, and understanding the roles of capacities, collocations, forces, and permanent causes in scientific explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause defined as antecedent invariably and unconditionally followed
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause of anything (in the relevant sense) is 'the antecedent, or the concurrence of antecedents, on which it is invariably and unconditionally consequent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that mere past succession is insufficient; the antecedent must be such that, given the present constitution of things, the consequent will always follow. Use this as the primary test for calling something a cause rather than a mere concomitant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish invariable sequence from unconditional causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Invariable sequence in past experience is not synonymous with causation unless the sequence is unconditional (i.e., would hold under all relevant suppositions about other facts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply counterfactual/conditional reasoning: ask whether the antecedent would still produce the consequent under varying other circumstances. Example: day/night succession is invariable historically but conditional on the sun's presence, so we do not call night the cause of day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity as 'unconditionalness' for causation
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of necessity in causation means unconditionalness—what will be, whatever suppositions we may make about all other things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating candidate causes, require belief (grounded in experience or warranted inference) that the antecedent will produce the consequent irrespective of irrelevant background changes; reject sequences that hold only because other antecedents co-occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude antecedents that are only conditionally invariable
rubrics_metrics.description: An antecedent that has always been followed by a consequent in our experience is not a cause if other evidence shows it might not always be so followed (i.e., it's only conditionally invariable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate other parts of experience for 'experimentum crucis' or cases that show the antecedent could exist without the consequent; if so, do not treat it as the invariable antecedent/true cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause as assemblage of positive conditions (omit superfluous negatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: If we confine 'cause' to positive conditions alone, then cause is 'the assemblage of positive conditions without the negative' — or, equivalently, 'subject to no other than negative conditions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When listing causes, prefer the minimal positive set of antecedents that suffice to produce the effect; negative conditions (absence of counteracting factors) are acknowledged but not counted among the positive constituents of the cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish immediate conditions (states/capacities) from causes that produced them
rubrics_metrics.description: Some antecedents produce a property or capacity in an object (a 'state of preparation') which later functions as a condition for another effect; the original cause produced the capacity, not the later effect directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reify capacities/state as independent substantive entities; treat them as reported assurances that the object will act in a certain way under further circumstances. In causal analysis, trace back to what produced the capacity when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause-effect temporal ordering (precedence criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although cause and effect can sometimes coincide in time (no perceptible interval), the cause does not precede the effect; when in doubt between two co-existent phenomena, we resolve cause vs effect by determining which preceded the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use temporal precedence (or evidence of prior occurrence) as a practical method for assigning causal direction among simultaneous phenomena; allow for practically instantaneous production but never effect preceding cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coexistence of multiple heterogeneous effects from one cause (properties/powers language)
rubrics_metrics.description: One phenomenon may be followed by diverse heterogeneous effects (e.g., the sun produces daylight, heat, celestial motions). We customarily describe this by attributing different 'properties' or 'powers' to the cause (gravitative, magnetic, calorific, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'properties' or 'powers' as convenient abstract names denoting regular connections between a cause and its different effects; these are heuristic/abridging devices and do not add empirical content beyond the uniformities they label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent (primeval) causes and limits of causal explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist permanent causes (sun, earth, elements, planetary motions) whose origin we cannot account for; co-existences of these primeval causes count as merely casual concurrences for us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that tracing effects back ultimately reaches primeval causes whose distribution may be irregular; do not assume universal laws of co-existence among effects unless grounded in common origin in primeval causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: All non-primeval phenomena are effects of prior causes (chain of invariable sequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every phenomenon that begins to exist is an effect, immediate or remote, of primitive facts or their combinations; the whole series of phenomena is the unconditional consequence of prior collocations of permanent causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In explanatory practice, attempt to situate phenomena within chains of antecedent-unconditional connections back to more general laws or primeval causes; view explanations as locating the antecedent assemblage that makes occurrence inevitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-existences among effects are not independent laws unless due to common cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Observable co-existences among effects generally do not constitute independent laws; they arise from identity or co-existence of their causes and are only unconditional when effects are different properties of the same cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing laws of co-existence, test whether the co-existence reduces to a shared cause; only treat co-existence as a law when it stems from different properties of a single natural agent (see 'Specific Properties of Kinds').

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation/Persistence of Force does not alter causation principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that different physical 'forces' are interconvertible (conservation of force) does not change the principle that each phenomenon has its set(s) of antecedents connected by invariable and unconditional sequence; the set of antecedents remains the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When integrating modern physical theory (e.g., conservation of force/motion) into causal analyses, continue to identify the relevant antecedent collocation; recognize the theoretical shift (forces as convertible modes) but maintain the same causal-accounting structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause comprises both presence of a force and a collocation/position
rubrics_metrics.description: In assembling the conditions constituting a cause, distinguish two elements: (1) the presence of a force (a changing antecedent), and (2) the collocation or position of objects required for the force to result in the specific phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For any production of an effect, ensure both: the requisite force (motion, chemical action, etc.) and the correct spatial/structural arrangement of materials. Example: a bonfire requires fuel/air (collocation) and chemical action (force).

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties/powers as useful abbreviations for connections between cause and multiple effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Naming attributes (color, hardness, gravitative property) is a powerful instrument of abridgment to denote the connection between different effects and the object that produces them, though such names explain nothing beyond the uniformities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use property-language to summarize regularities but avoid treating these labels as explanatory primitives; always be prepared to analyze the specific antecedents that ground each named property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish instantaneous phenomena from persistent effects requiring continuous cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Some phenomena are instantaneous (e.g., illumination at a point) and require continual reproduction by their causes, whereas other effects, once produced (e.g., a plowshare), continue without the ongoing presence of the original agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether an effect's continuance requires ongoing positive conditions or only negative ones (absence of counteracting forces); phrase causation appropriately (reproduce vs maintain) according to whether renewal by the cause is needed.
